title: Coral and the Bridge
premise: In 1911, Ansel Sandoval carries a courier's satchel of coded dispatches for a republic collapsing under its own generals, and when the army requisitions the river town of Coral's Bridge, the ledger hidden inside his late mentor's house — a ledger naming every family that sheltered dissidents — becomes both evidence and death warrant. Ansel and Coral Vane, the mentor's daughter who has spent fifteen years pretending her father was an ordinary customs clerk, must move the ledger past three checkpoints before New Year's amnesty expires and the names are burned with the town's records. Along the way Ansel must choose between the loyalty that kept him alive and the truth that could save two hundred families, while Coral confronts what her father really did in the silences she inherited. The book ends at the third checkpoint on New Year's Eve: Ansel surrenders himself as the courier the army has hunted for fifteen years, buying Coral time to carry the ledger across the bridge to the foreign consul, and the final chapter shows the names read aloud a year later from a rebuilt courthouse steps.
about_author: Jonah Pemberton is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing confiscated state records before turning to fiction. They write historical novels about ordinary people caught holding dangerous paper.

chapters.title: The Weight of Paper
chapters.summary: Ansel Sandoval arrives in Coral's Bridge on a winter mail boat, carrying diplomatic dispatches he no longer believes in. POV: Ansel. The beat is weary duty — he plans one last delivery and retirement, unaware the town he chose is about to be swallowed by the war it escaped.

chapters.title: A House Full of Silences
chapters.summary: Coral Vane keeps her father's customs house like a museum of respectable lies, dusting ledgers she has never dared open. POV: Coral. The emotional beat is inherited denial; she recognizes Ansel as her father's old courier and feels the first crack in fifteen years of chosen ignorance.

chapters.title: Requisition
chapters.summary: At dawn, Colonel Ferran's troops occupy the town, billeting soldiers in homes and sealing the records office. POV: Ansel. The beat is cold shock — he watches the machinery he once served turn on civilians, and realizes his satchel's codes match the seals now going up around him.

chapters.title: What Father Kept
chapters.summary: Searching her father's study for requisition papers, Coral finds a false-backed drawer and the ledger: two hundred names, dates, safe houses. POV: Coral. The beat is vertigo — grief curdling into betrayal as she understands her childhood home was a station on an underground railroad.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints
chapters.summary: Ansel maps the town's exits: the north road checkpoint, the river barge inspection, and the bridge itself, where Ferran has posted his most suspicious sergeant. POV: Ansel. The beat is grim calculation; he tells Coral the ledger cannot stay, and she refuses to let it be destroyed instead.

chapters.title: The Sergeant's Memory
chapters.summary: Sergeant Ivo Rask, posted at the bridge, recognizes Ansel's face from a fifteen-year-old wanted circular — but says nothing, because Ansel once carried a pardon that saved Rask's brother. POV: Rask. The beat is divided loyalty; the hunter owes the hunted a debt he cannot repay openly.

chapters.title: Billeted
chapters.summary: Soldiers quartered in the customs house find Coral's hospitality suffocating and her questions dangerous; Lieutenant Osta begins pulling files on the Vane family. POV: Coral. The beat is claustrophobic performance — she serves dinner to men hunting her father's ghost.

chapters.title: The Old Cipher
chapters.summary: Ansel decodes the ledger's marginal marks and discovers his own name among the couriers, plus a dead-drop schedule that still functions. POV: Ansel. The beat is reluctant reawakening — the network may be dead, but its routes through the marshes are not.

chapters.title: Amnesty Expires at Midnight
chapters.summary: Ferran announces that on New Year's Eve all pre-war cases close permanently: records burned, names struck, no testimony ever admissible again. POV: Ansel. The beat is a ticking clock made law — after midnight, the ledger becomes worthless paper and the families lose their only proof.

chapters.title: Osta's Question
chapters.summary: Lieutenant Osta interviews Coral about her father's 'customs business,' laying out discrepancies like cards. POV: Coral. The beat is terror managed into poise; she lies well for the first time in her life and hates how easily it comes.

chapters.title: The Marsh Route
chapters.summary: Ansel tests the old smuggler's path through the frozen marshes and finds it watched; he barely escapes a patrol, twisting an ankle that slows everything after. POV: Ansel. The beat is humbling — the routes he trusted have aged as badly as he has.

chapters.title: Rask's Debt
chapters.summary: Rask privately warns Ansel that Osta has requested the old courier files from the capital. POV: Rask. The beat is a debt called in — Rask gives him two days, not out of mercy, but because he needs to know which man he served all those years ago.

chapters.title: Names, Not Numbers
chapters.summary: Coral reads the ledger cover to cover and finds her schoolteacher, her godmother, the ferryman — people who were kind to a fatherless girl. POV: Coral. The beat is transformation; denial burns off and she commits to carrying the names herself if Ansel falls.

chapters.title: The Barge Gambit
chapters.summary: They hide the ledger in a coal shipment bound downriver, but Osta orders random cargo breaks and the barge is held at the second checkpoint. POV: alternating Ansel and Coral. The beat is hope punctured — plan one dies publicly, and now the army knows someone is moving something.

chapters.title: Interrogation by Lamplight
chapters.summary: Osta detains Coral overnight, circling her father's history while she holds to the customs-clerk story. POV: Coral. The beat is endurance — she discovers her father trained her for this without ever telling her, every silence a rehearsal.

chapters.title: The Confession at the Lockhouse
chapters.summary: Ansel confesses to Coral that he abandoned her father on the last mission, choosing the dispatches over the man. POV: Ansel. The beat is shame finally spoken; Coral's forgiveness is conditional — he will spend it at the bridge.

chapters.title: Ferran's Trap
chapters.summary: Ferran announces the bridge closes entirely on New Year's Eve except for one inspected crossing at dusk — a trap baited with exactly the deadline they face. POV: Ansel. The beat is checkmate approaching; every route is closed except the one designed to catch them.

chapters.title: Two Couriers
chapters.summary: Coral proposes the split: she takes the ledger toward the bridge while Ansel lets himself be identified as the legendary courier, drawing every eye. POV: Coral. The beat is resolve — the daughter of silences chooses to become the loudest thing in town.

chapters.title: New Year's Eve
chapters.summary: Fireworks mask their movements; Coral walks the ledger toward the consulate barge while Ansel presents himself at the bridge checkpoint. POV: alternating. The beat is breathless convergence — fifteen years of hiding end in one hour of exposure.

chapters.title: The Third Checkpoint
chapters.summary: Ansel surrenders, claiming sole responsibility, while Rask must choose: arrest the man who saved his brother or stall the search long enough. POV: Rask. The beat is the climax of loyalty vs. truth — Rask delays the alarm, then arrests Ansel anyway, weeping.

chapters.title: Across the Water
chapters.summary: Coral reaches the foreign consul as midnight strikes, handing over the ledger seconds before amnesty voids it; behind her, the town hears Ansel's name read from the arrest roll. POV: Coral. The beat is triumph laced with cost — the names are safe, and the man who carried them is not.

chapters.title: Read Aloud
chapters.summary: One year later, at the rebuilt courthouse, the two hundred names are read publicly; Coral stands beside a paroled Ansel, and Rask, dismissed from the army, listens from the crowd. POV: Coral. The beat is resolution — memory outlived the republic that tried to burn it, and silence finally gives way to speech.
